Nāgārjuna
Bud. philosopher founder of the Mādhyamika school; though very few works of his are available in Sanskrit, several works are preserved in Tibetan an. Chinese translations. He is often confused with the later Tāntric writer in Tibetan traditions. Max Walleser, who analysed the conflicting traditional accounts, doubted the very existence of the Buddhist master (Life of Nāgārjuna from Tibetan an. Chinese Sources, Asia Major, 1923); Winternitz on the other hand suggests that [Page012-a. the Bud. philosopher, the Tāntric writer, the medical writer an. the alchemist were four different men (HIL. II. 344n). Kumārajīva who introduced Nāgārjuna to Chin., an. translated into Chinese several of his works in the 4th Cent. A. D. has written a legendary biography of Nāgārjuna (Taisho 2087). Nāgārjuna was born a. a Brahmin in South India; with his knowledge in magic he led a life of lust an. passion until he joined the Buddhist order. Hiuan-tsang mentions him a. a contemporary of Aśvaghoṣa, an. according to the Rājataraṅgiṇī, he was a. contemporary of Kaniṣka. Tradition makes him a friend of the Śātavāhana king who built a. monastery for him a. Śrīparvata; this king is generally identified with Gautamīputra Śātakarṇī or king Hāla of Gāthāsaptaśatī fame; recent excavations a. Nāgārjunakoṇḍa support Nāgārjuna's association with South India. He is said to have obtained the Prajñāpāramitāsūtras from a Nāga chief. He prob. flourished between the first an. second centuries A. D. (150-250 according to Nakamura) an. was the teacher of Āryadeva.
According to Kumārajīva's biography Nāgārjuna is the a. of (1) Upadeśa in 100,000 gāthās, (2) Buddhamārgālaṅkāra Śāśtra in 5000 gāthās, (3) Mahākaruṇopāyaśāstra in 5000 gāthās, (4) Madhyamakaśāstra in 500 gāthās an. (5) the Akutobhayaśāstra in 100,000 gāthās. The identity of these is not clear.
On Nāgārjuna see Max Walleser, Life of Nāgārjuna; Wint. HIL. II. 341-51; Etienne Lamotte, La Traite de la Grande Vertu de Sagesse de [Page012-b] Nāgārjuna, Vol.. I. II. Louvain 1944, 1949; K. V. Ramanan, Nāgārjuna's Philosophy. Bharatiya Vidya Prakashan Varanasi 1, 1971; T. R. V. Murti, The Central Philosophy of Buddhism, Allen an. Unwin, 1955; Merwyn Sprung (ed.), Problems of Two Truths in Buddhism an. Vedanta, Reidel Publishing C.., 1973; Warder, Indian Buddhism, Motilal Banarsidass, Delhi, 1970, p.. 374-92; K.
